about: Sections of an essay on romance by Joel (first person). In each, the sentences listed under "changed" were just rewritten; the rest is the essay as it stands. Read each section as it stands, with its heading.

texts.heading: Labels Are Descriptive, Not Prescriptive
changed: The full conversation about all that is so big that almost nobody would have casual sex if they took it seriously.
sentences: Here’s the funny thing about labels: you can call someone your boyfriend or girlfriend for years and still have one foot out the door, but the word at least shows pretty fast whether you both think you’re in the same relationship.
True commitment grows out of relational depth, not a label we put on it.
If we spend hours telling each other our deepest longings and fears, then I’ll naturally be ready to help when you need me.
I don’t need to promise that on paper, and if I did, that would be more like a red flag.
If someone says “I love you, I feel you, I’m here for you,” yet they hardly ever talk to you about what matters, that’s an even more obvious red flag.
The person getting more of what they want may think the arrangement is fulfilling, but usually they’re just less aware that it isn’t.
In college I had a friend with four girlfriends who boasted about it to girls while trying to get a fifth.
I asked him, “But are you really happy?”
He said, “No, dude, I’m miserable and empty inside.”
I can’t decide what is okay for anybody else.
I can say that most people who defend casual sex are not being very honest with themselves about pregnancy, attachment, or what they might owe the person afterward.
The full conversation about all that is so big that almost nobody would have casual sex if they took it seriously.
Which is why almost nobody has the full conversation.
Outside a loving poly community or tribe, I think honest casual sex is almost impossible.

If you want something closer to “casual love-making” without quite so many ways to damage each other, you probably need to find a free-love community where the people aren’t disposable, the bonds can be acknowledged, and any children have a village.

But if the community is specifically designed to prioritize free love, you might find it attracts people who have traumas that produce trouble with connecting deeply, as ex-Tamera leader, Martin Winiecki wrote about after leaving recently.

texts.heading: Peeking thru the window
changed: You may not see their jealousy, abandonment, and possessiveness, or whether the “I’m so much better than I used to be” story survives, until there is stress and entanglement.
sentences: You can also bring the person to a party, around your friends and family and see how they act, or take them to activities you enjoy and see if they really enjoy them too (although if they seem to enjoy every single one of them, they might be pretending).
Try doing what you would normally do in your day alone, but with them, and see if it feels weird.
Are they wondering why you spend hours playing with your cat?
Do they look bored, like they’d rather just hit you up later for some fun?
See their negative side first too.
If there is no negative side, that’s a red flag for fakery.
Ask whether the spiritual story they tell about themselves survives an inconvenient PMS afternoon.
How recent is the healing story—two months or two years?
You may not see their jealousy, abandonment, and possessiveness, or whether the “I’m so much better than I used to be” story survives, until there is stress and entanglement.
By then, of course, you’re stressed and entangled. 😆
Sometimes the only thing I have is a little “wait” feeling.
If I'm about to ignore a question because I really want this to work, that "wait" is enough reason for me to ask the question before I keep going.
If they’re nasty to their friends, family, or other people, assume they will eventually be nasty to you.
We mostly seem to get attracted to the inner-child part because we’re coming from our inner child and we want to have fun.
But you also need to find out whether there is a healthy adult there before you’re too bonded to want the answer.

texts.heading: Seeing idealization right
changed: Although if something severe is happening, sometimes a demand or boundary is necessary too.
sentences: You can see something in a person before she fully lives it, but then you have to ask her:
“I see this in you, and I think it’s special.
Do you wanna reach for it together?”
If she says no, forget it.
You’re in la la land.
If she says yes, ask what is blocking her.
Is the block more than you can handle?
Or does she mostly need somebody to join her on the journey and believe in her?
Partners should help each other grow.
Who else is going to do it?
Your mom and dad?
You’re already grown to them.
Everybody else will usually be a smaller influence, so you’d better choose someone who helps you grow well.
Like the FM Laeti song down in the Twin Flames section says, “Inspire her to see the best in herself, actualize that.”
Although if something severe is happening, sometimes a demand or boundary is necessary too.

texts.heading: Babies growing up again
changed: Nobody has to be completely healed before entering a relationship, but I think that as we learn more about ourselves through the crucible, we should naturally raise our standards.
I already said that before dating, the present-day adult has to be able to parent whatever intimacy wakes up inside you.
sentences: Nobody has to be completely healed before entering a relationship, but I think that as we learn more about ourselves through the crucible, we should naturally raise our standards.
Maybe at first we need the drama to access our primal emotions, but after years of that, we’re exhausted by what we previously hoped to find.
At the very least, there needs to be honesty, real effort at improving, and some ability to stop blaming everybody else for your own problems.
I already said that before dating, the present-day adult has to be able to parent whatever intimacy wakes up inside you.
Once you’re together, more of that stuff comes out.
Inner-child reparenting means parenting the child part instead of surreptitiously hiring the partner for the job.
It can get pretty entitled when you expect your partner to know what you need without being told.
You may barely see your own pattern, and then deny it instead of taking responsibility when they point it out.

texts.heading: Jealousy on trial
changed: How much attention to other people actually feels healthy is something every couple has to work out for themselves.
sentences: Jealousy is always insecurity, but sometimes that insecurity can be an important indicator that the relationship actually is not secure, rather than just a remembered script from childhood.
Although, either way, it can become a self-fulfilling prophecy.
Instead of stewing in jealousy and throwing out microaggressions now and then, speak your heart without hiding the insecurity behind anger, as in the above video I found on IG.
In a monogamous relationship, you might say:
“I notice you pay attention to this other girl more than me, and it makes me feel unloved and insecure.
Can we talk about it?
Do you really want to explore things with her?
If so that’s fine, but don’t make the decision lightly, because it’s irreversible.”
Maybe he really is neglecting you or wanting to be with someone else.
Maybe the “attention” was one glance and your baseline insecurity inflated it into a threat that it wasn’t.
That part should not be projected onto your partner.
How much attention to other people actually feels healthy is something every couple has to work out for themselves.
I do believe two people can choose sexual exclusivity honestly.
They can admit that attraction to other people exists and decide not to act on it each day.
And even better than simply suppressing it, they can put it to work.
I agree with Esther Perel, who writes that this sexual energy felt outside the relationship can be used and redirected into the relationship to make it more alive.

texts.heading: Tough Love
changed: A romance that actually works is rare, and that’s probably why romantic love has been seen with suspicion as a destabilizing force throughout history.
That spirit is like the universe living its desire to know itself through us, which might be why we see ourselves in ways we couldn’t imagine before.
Like Somé, they wore rose-colored glasses too and taught me that everybody was basically good.
sentences: Romantic love is not easy, and the things that actually make it work are not very marketable.
I can’t sell you the fix with one click or one monthly subscription to my love class.
(Just kidding, click here!)
A romance that actually works is rare, and that’s probably why romantic love has been seen with suspicion as a destabilizing force throughout history.
One of the best books that makes that point today might be the one I was reading with Key: The Spirit of Intimacy, by Sobonfu Somé.
Somé came from the Dagara tribe in Burkina Faso.
To her people, marriage is an arranged, ritualized spiritual and communal responsibility.
They’re suspicious of romance.
But one of her ideas fits what I’m trying to say: the relationship is bigger and more important than the egos in it.
She calls it the spirit of the relationship.
That spirit is like the universe living its desire to know itself through us, which might be why we see ourselves in ways we couldn’t imagine before.
Nobody can command the spirit to remain.
At our best, we serve it and listen for what Spirit wants to change.
When we start thinking we own it or deserve it, that presumptuousness tends to push it away.
My parents agreed with Somé that community matters and that we serve Spirit.
They were also not romantic, though they were loving and poly.
I actually wished they were in love with each other, I guess, although I couldn’t have articulated that since I didn’t even have that concept at the time.
Like Somé, they wore rose-colored glasses too and taught me that everybody was basically good.

So I learned something about love and community, but not how hard romance is without a community around it, or how much damage basically good people can do when their fears, trauma, and undeveloped parts take over.
It took me many decades to figure out what probably everyone else already knows: real private pathology exists.
But pathology festers when the environment is perfect for it.
The dominant culture hermetically seals two people together and calls that a luxurious privacy.
It tells them that sealed room should provide all the fresh air you’d get from a lover, family, community, therapist, and so on.
Then it treats the predictable failure as privately caused as well, like mold that grows out of nowhere.
